articles.title: India vs China Self-Propelled Artillery: Why a Nearly 30x Gap Should Worry Indian Defence Planners
articles.text:
When it comes to self-propelled artillery — mobile, armoured gun systems that can fire and rapidly relocate to avoid counter-battery strikes — India’s inventory looks starkly thin next to China’s. India currently fields around 100 K9 Vajra-T self-propelled howitzers, while China’s People’s Liberation Army operates a sprawling fleet of roughly 2,900–3,000 units across six major systems: the PLZ-05, PCL-181, PLZ-07, PLL-09, PCL-171, and PCL-161. That’s a gap of nearly 30 times in raw numbers — a disparity that matters a great deal in any scenario involving sustained, high-tempo ground combat along a contested border.
The Indian Army currently operates around 100 K9 Vajra-T units, an Indian adaptation of South Korea’s K9 Thunder 155mm/52-calibre self-propelled howitzer manufactured domestically by Larsen & Toubro under a technology transfer agreement with Hanwha Aerospace. The first contract for 100 howitzers was signed in 2017 for roughly ₹4,500 crore and completed ahead of schedule by 2021, with these systems primarily deployed in desert regions along the western border.
Expansion is underway but still modest relative to the scale of the gap. A follow-on order for another 100 guns, valued at around ₹7,629 crore, was approved in late 2023/2024, and a further proposal — if sanctioned — would push the total number of K9 Vajra units ordered past 500. This larger, roughly ₹23,000 crore procurement plan was under review by the Defence Procurement Board as of mid-2026, reflecting growing recognition within the defence establishment of the need to close this gap, particularly given readiness requirements along both the western border and the Line of Actual Control with China.
China’s Self-Propelled Artillery Fleet: Numbers and Variety
China’s advantage isn’t just in scale — it’s also in the sheer diversity of systems fielded, spanning tracked and wheeled platforms across multiple calibres:
PLZ-05: A 155mm tracked self-propelled howitzer produced from 2003 to 2025, capable of firing extended-range munitions out to 50–60 km depending on ammunition type, and designed to replace older Chinese towed and self-propelled guns.
PLZ-07: A 122mm tracked self-propelled howitzer first unveiled in 2009, built on a ZBD-04 infantry fighting vehicle chassis with a firing range up to 27 km using rocket-assisted ammunition.
PCL-171: A lightweight, 122mm assault-vehicle-mounted self-propelled howitzer that entered service in 2020, offering firing ranges up to 40 km with extended-range projectiles and designed as a more mobile complement to the larger PCL-161.
PLL-09: A 122mm self-propelled gun mounted on the wheeled Type 08 (ZBL-08) armoured personnel carrier chassis, with at least 600 units fielded and production continuing.
PCL-181: A truck-mounted 155mm wheeled self-propelled gun, with more than 600 units now in PLA service and production still ongoing.
PCL-161: A truck-chassis-mounted 122mm self-propelled howitzer that, alongside PCL-171, forms part of China’s push toward lighter, faster-deploying wheeled artillery systems.
Beyond these six systems, China’s broader self-propelled gun-mortar inventory is even larger still, with production of the 120mm PLL-05 mortar carrier alone reportedly exceeding 1,500 units. Collectively, independent estimates placing China’s combined self-propelled artillery fleet across these platforms in the range of roughly 2,900–3,000 units are broadly consistent with the scale suggested by publicly available production figures for individual systems.
Why Raw Numbers in Self-Propelled Artillery Matter
Self-propelled artillery’s core advantage over towed guns is survivability and tempo: a mobile platform can fire and relocate within minutes, evading the counter-battery radar and precision strikes that would quickly destroy a static towed gun position. In a prolonged, high-intensity conflict — particularly across the kind of extended, mountainous frontage India shares with China along the LAC — the side with a deeper bench of mobile, shoot-and-scoot artillery systems retains firepower and sustainment advantages that towed artillery simply cannot match.
A nearly 30x numerical gap doesn’t mean China’s artillery is 30 times more effective in every engagement — terrain, logistics, doctrine, and force concentration all matter enormously. But it does mean China has substantially greater depth to sustain artillery operations across multiple fronts simultaneously, replace losses, and rotate units without depleting frontline firepower — a strategic cushion India’s current inventory does not yet provide.
Closing the Gap: What’s Next for India
The trajectory suggests India is aware of the shortfall. Beyond the K9 Vajra-T expansion, discussions around India’s artillery modernisation have also touched on reviving indigenous programmes like the shelved Bhim self-propelled howitzer, which combined the Arjun tank chassis with a 155mm turret, though geopolitical and procurement hurdles previously stalled that effort. Whether through accelerated K9 Vajra-T orders, a revived indigenous programme, or a mix of both, meaningfully narrowing this gap will likely take a sustained, decade-scale procurement effort rather than any single contract.

articles.title: Kalavinka Technologies Unveils AI-Powered Nyx MK-I Loitering Munition for GPS-Denied Warfare
articles.text:
India’s rapidly expanding defence startup ecosystem has taken another significant step forward with Kalavinka Technologies unveiling the Nyx MK-I, an indigenous autonomous loitering munition designed to operate in highly contested and GPS-denied environments. Developed by engineers from the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur, the system combines artificial intelligence, autonomous navigation and low-cost manufacturing to address the evolving requirements of modern battlefields.
The Nyx MK-I reflects the increasing role of Indian startups in developing advanced military technologies traditionally dominated by large defence companies. With its emphasis on autonomy, scalability and indigenous engineering, the platform aligns closely with India’s Aatmanirbhar Bharat initiative and the armed forces’ growing focus on network-centric warfare.
A defining feature of the Nyx MK-I is its fire-and-forget autonomous operation. Unlike many conventional unmanned systems that depend on continuous communication links or Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) such as GPS, the Nyx MK-I relies on onboard sensor-based navigation and embedded artificial intelligence. This enables the munition to continue its mission even in environments where satellite navigation is unavailable or deliberately disrupted through electronic warfare.
Such capability is becoming increasingly important as modern conflicts have demonstrated the widespread use of GPS jamming and spoofing technologies. Autonomous navigation reduces dependence on vulnerable external signals and enhances the platform’s survivability against sophisticated electronic attack systems.
Kalavinka Technologies has also emphasised that the Nyx MK-I has been engineered entirely in-house, covering every stage of development from computer-aided design (CAD) and aerodynamic simulations to embedded computing architecture and software integration. This level of indigenous development not only strengthens domestic technological capabilities but also reduces dependence on foreign intellectual property and critical components.
The loitering munition has been designed to conduct precision strikes against soft targets, forward enemy positions and vulnerable tactical assets. Loitering munitions combine the functions of reconnaissance drones and precision-guided weapons by searching for targets over a designated area before diving onto them once identified. This provides commanders with greater operational flexibility compared to conventional artillery or missile systems, particularly when engaging time-sensitive or mobile targets.
Another important aspect of the Nyx MK-I is its low-cost, attritable design philosophy. Rather than focusing on building a small number of expensive platforms, the system has been designed for affordable mass production. Attritable systems are intended to be cost-effective enough that they can be deployed in large numbers without imposing excessive financial burdens if individual units are lost during combat.
This approach is increasingly shaping military procurement worldwide, where quantity and operational flexibility are viewed as critical advantages in high-intensity conflicts.
The Nyx MK-I has also been developed with swarm warfare in mind. According to Kalavinka Technologies, multiple loitering munitions can operate together in coordinated attacks, overwhelming enemy air defence systems through simultaneous engagements from different directions. Swarming tactics are widely regarded as one of the most disruptive trends in modern warfare because they complicate an adversary’s ability to detect, track and intercept numerous incoming threats at once.
Artificial intelligence plays a central role in enabling such operations by allowing autonomous coordination between multiple platforms while reducing operator workload.
The system’s emphasis on operating in electronic warfare environments further reflects lessons emerging from recent conflicts, where the electromagnetic spectrum has become as contested as the physical battlefield. By reducing dependence on continuous communications and satellite navigation, the Nyx MK-I is intended to maintain operational effectiveness even in heavily jammed environments where conventional drones may struggle to complete their missions.
The unveiling of the Nyx MK-I also highlights the growing contribution of Indian startups to the country’s defence innovation ecosystem. Over the past few years, startups have increasingly entered areas such as unmanned aerial systems, artificial intelligence, robotics, autonomous vehicles and advanced sensors, complementing the efforts of the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), public sector enterprises and established private defence manufacturers.
Government initiatives supporting innovation, including the Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) programme, have created new opportunities for startups to develop technologies tailored to the operational requirements of the Indian Armed Forces.
As militaries worldwide invest heavily in autonomous systems, AI-enabled loitering munitions are expected to become a key component of future battlefield operations. Their ability to deliver precision strikes, operate in contested environments and conduct coordinated swarm attacks makes them valuable assets for both conventional and asymmetric warfare scenarios.

articles.title: Bhargavastra’s Command and Control Centre: Inside the Radar and Sensor Suite Powering India’s Counter-Drone Shield
articles.text:
Solar Defence and Aerospace Ltd’s (SDAL) Bhargavastra counter-swarm drone system has drawn attention not just for its micro-missile interceptors, but for the sophisticated Command and Control Centre that ties the entire platform together. Social media posts around the system’s recent Nagpur demonstration have pointed to Data Patterns’ Phantom Hunter 2 Air Defence Fire Control Radar (ADFCR) as part of the sensor mix inside that vehicle-mounted control hub — a detail worth unpacking alongside what has been officially confirmed about the system.
What’s Confirmed About Bhargavastra’s Command and Control Centre
During the July 24 demonstration at SDAL’s Nagpur facility, the Bhargavastra weapon system was shown in its full configuration, comprising a Command & Control Vehicle (CCV) equipped with radar, EO/IR and RF detectors integrated with the C4I system, alongside a launcher vehicle carrying all the launch tubes This Command-and-Control Centre incorporates an advanced C4I architecture built around a radar capable of detecting UAVs up to 10 km away, an Electro-Optical/Infrared (EO/IR) surveillance system, and passive RF sensors.<
>During the trial, SDAL flew a swarm of drones that were successfully detected by the radar, EO/IR, and RF detectors, after which the C4I system displayed a complete situational awareness picture and generated a drone attack alert. The launcher was then assigned targets by the C4I system, and the full firing sequence was demonstrated to the visiting Army team.</cite>
The Data Patterns Connection: Phantom Hunter Radar Family
While official SDAL and Army statements around the Nagpur demonstration describe the radar generically, India’s homegrown radar maker Data Patterns has developed a relevant product line that fits this description closely. Data Patterns’ Air Defence Fire Control Radar (ADFCR) is a dual-vehicle system combining the Phantom Hunter X-band search radar with the Phantom Tracker Ka-band track radar. The ADFCR is a ground-based air defence system designed for short to very-short-range threats in all-weather conditions, built to serve the Indian Army and Air Defence units.
Some posts circulating on social media around the Bhargavastra demonstration have specifically referenced a “Phantom Hunter 2” variant as part of the Command and Control Centre’s sensor suite. This specific pairing has not yet been confirmed in official SDAL statements, ANI coverage, or other mainstream defence reporting on the Nagpur trial, so it should currently be treated as an unverified detail from social media rather than an established fact, pending confirmation from SDAL or Data Patterns.
How the Sensor Suite Enables Swarm Detection
Bhargavastra’s command and control setup pairs radar capable of detecting tiny drones from 6 to 10 km away with cameras and infrared sensors for tracking and identification, feeding into a comprehensive battlefield-view system that helps operators make rapid decisions.The system can also integrate with existing military networks such as Akashteer and the Integrated Air Command and Control System, enabling network-centric operation alongside India’s broader air defence grid.
When Bhargavastra detects a small hostile drone more than six kilometres out, its full-authority fire control system deploys micro-rockets or micro-missiles directed toward the threat, while low radar-cross-section targets are additionally picked up through the embedded EO/IR sensor.
What to Watch Next
As Bhargavastra moves toward the completion of its internal trials within the next two to three months, further official disclosures are likely to clarify the exact radar and sensor components used in its Command and Control Centre, including whether Data Patterns’ Phantom Hunter family is indeed part of the configuration. Until an official confirmation from SDAL, Data Patterns, or the Ministry of Defence emerges, this specific radar-integration detail should be read as a reported claim rather than a verified specification.

articles.title: RedSaffron Aerospace Unveils DHVANI 2.0, a Quad-Tailsitter VTOL Interceptor Targeting 700 km/h Speeds
articles.text:
Indian aerospace startup RedSaffron Aerospace has announced its latest hard-kill counter-UAS platform, DHVANI 2.0, a high-speed quad-tailsitter VTOL kinetic interceptor designed to neutralise hostile drones through direct impact rather than jamming or spoofing. The company says it is preparing for high-velocity flight testing aimed at breaking the 700 km/h barrier, positioning DHVANI 2.0 as one of the fastest interceptor-class drones to emerge from India’s private defence-tech ecosystem.
According to RedSaffron Aerospace, DHVANI 2.0 is built as a hard-kill counter-UAS (Unmanned Aerial System) interceptor — meaning it is designed to physically destroy incoming hostile drones through direct kinetic impact, rather than relying on electronic warfare methods like jamming or GPS spoofing. This approach mirrors the broader trend across India’s counter-drone sector, where multiple companies are betting on physical interception as the more reliable answer to autonomous, jam-resistant drone threats.
The company describes DHVANI 2.0 as engineered specifically for tactical flight at the “absolute physical limits” of what current autonomous aerial systems can achieve, with an upcoming test campaign built around pushing sustained speeds past 700 km/h.
Quad-Tailsitter VTOL: Why the Architecture Matters
DHVANI 2.0 uses a quad-tailsitter Vertical Take-Off and Landing (VTOL) configuration — an aircraft design that takes off and lands standing upright on its tail before rotating into a horizontal, fixed-wing-style flight orientation for high-speed cruise and pursuit. This class of aircraft is mechanically simpler than tilt-rotor or tilt-wing VTOL designs since it typically avoids complex rotating mechanisms, though it is aerodynamically more demanding to control during hover and the transition between vertical and horizontal flight.
RedSaffron says this “zero-infrastructure” approach lets DHVANI 2.0 deploy immediately from virtually any location, without requiring launch catapults, runways, or other fixed infrastructure — a significant operational advantage for rapid-response counter-drone deployment in the field, forward operating bases, or contested terrain where traditional airstrips aren’t available.
Engineering Behind the 700 km/h Target
To reach and sustain high-velocity flight, RedSaffron says DHVANI 2.0 combines a precision-molded monocoque airframe with high-frequency power electronics, an engineering pairing intended to suppress high-speed flutter — the potentially destructive vibration that can occur in aircraft structures at high velocities — while enabling extreme acceleration. A monocoque design, where the outer skin bears much of the structural load, is typically favoured in high-performance aircraft for its strength-to-weight efficiency, which matters directly for an interceptor drone that needs both speed and manoeuvrability.
Autonomous Interception in Contested, GPS-Denied Airspace
Beyond raw speed, RedSaffron is positioning DHVANI 2.0 as capable of full autonomous operation in electronic-warfare-contested environments. The company says the platform uses real-time onboard vision-based tracking combined with GNSS-denied Simultaneous Localisation and Mapping (SLAM) navigation, allowing it to detect, track, and pursue aerial targets even when satellite navigation signals are jammed or unavailable — a capability increasingly seen as essential given how modern drone warfare has shown that GPS-dependent systems can be neutralised through electronic countermeasures.
Part of a Broader Wave of Indigenous Counter-Drone Development
RedSaffron’s announcement adds to a fast-growing field of Indian counter-UAS platforms emerging from both established defence manufacturers and newer startups, as India accelerates efforts toward self-reliant, hard-kill solutions against drone swarms and loitering munitions. The company describes DHVANI 2.0 as 100% indigenously engineered, aligning with the broader Aatmanirbhar Bharat push across India’s defence-tech sector to reduce dependence on imported systems for critical low-altitude airspace defence — an area increasingly described as central to “modern economic warfare” given how weaponised drones can target infrastructure well below the threshold of conventional armed conflict.

articles.title: Could Adani’s Embraer Partnership Disrupt India’s Airline Market? Here’s What the Numbers Say
articles.text:
The strategic partnership between the Adani Group and Brazilian aircraft manufacturer Embraer has sparked speculation that the Indian conglomerate could eventually enter the commercial airline business. While neither company has officially announced plans for a scheduled passenger airline, industry observers believe that such a move would naturally complement the partnership’s objective of creating an Embraer regional aircraft ecosystem and final assembly line in India.
If Adani were to launch an airline, it could become the launch customer for Embraer aircraft assembled domestically, creating a vertically integrated aviation ecosystem spanning airports, aircraft manufacturing, maintenance, pilot training, ground handling and airline operations.
Such an arrangement would provide Embraer with an immediate domestic customer while allowing Adani to optimise aircraft support infrastructure across its growing aviation portfolio.
However, despite the strategic advantages, an all-Embraer fleet is unlikely to fundamentally replace the Airbus A320 or Boeing 737 families that currently dominate India’s commercial aviation market.
India’s domestic airline industry is built around dense trunk routes connecting metropolitan cities such as Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Chennai. These sectors generate exceptionally high passenger volumes, making aircraft like the Airbus A320neo and Boeing 737 MAX the most economically efficient choices. With seating capacities typically ranging from 180 to over 230 passengers, these narrow-body aircraft achieve some of the world’s lowest cost per available seat kilometre (CASK) when operated at high load factors.
Embraer’s commercial aircraft portfolio serves a different segment of the market.
Its latest E-Jet E2 family, including the E175-E2, E190-E2 and E195-E2, typically accommodates between 80 and 146 passengers, positioning the aircraft between traditional regional turboprops and larger narrow-body jets.
Rather than competing head-on with the A320 on India’s busiest routes, Embraer aircraft are ideally suited to connecting Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities, where passenger demand often cannot consistently fill larger aircraft.
This market represents one of India’s fastest-growing aviation opportunities.
Government initiatives such as UDAN (Ude Desh ka Aam Naagrik) have expanded air connectivity to smaller cities, but many routes remain too thin to support daily A320 operations. On these sectors, airlines frequently face the choice of operating larger aircraft with low passenger loads or abandoning the route altogether.
An Embraer-based fleet changes this equation.
With significantly lower trip costs, airlines require fewer passengers to achieve profitability. A route carrying 90 to 110 passengers may be commercially unattractive for an A320 but could be economically sustainable using an Embraer E195-E2.
This flexibility would allow Adani to open numerous direct city pairs that currently lack viable commercial service while simultaneously feeding passengers into its airport network.
The strategy becomes even more compelling when viewed alongside Adani’s broader aviation assets.
The group already operates several major airports, including Mumbai, Navi Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Jaipur, Lucknow, Guwahati, Mangaluru and Thiruvananthapuram. Combined with investments in ground handling, maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) infrastructure, cargo operations and aviation training, an Embraer-focused airline could leverage substantial operational efficiencies unavailable to most competitors.
Shorter turnaround times, integrated maintenance support and optimised airport slot management could reduce operating costs further while improving aircraft utilisation.
From a financial perspective, Embraer aircraft also require a lower capital investment.
An E195-E2 costs considerably less than an Airbus A320neo, reducing financing requirements for fleet expansion. This makes regional fleet growth more manageable, particularly during the early years of an airline’s operations.
Operating economics tell a similarly nuanced story.
On an absolute basis, an Embraer regional jet consumes less fuel, incurs lower landing charges and generally costs less to operate on each individual flight than an A320neo.
However, because it carries fewer passengers, its cost per available seat kilometre (CASK) can exceed that of a fully occupied A320 on dense routes. This is why Embraer aircraft are not designed to replace larger narrow-body jets but rather to serve markets where demand does not justify them.
The latest E2 family also benefits from highly efficient next-generation engines and aerodynamic improvements that deliver significantly better fuel efficiency than earlier regional jet designs. While Pratt & Whitney’s geared turbofan (GTF) engine family has experienced durability challenges across several operators worldwide, the aircraft itself remains among the most fuel-efficient in its market segment.
Comparisons with aircraft such as the Boeing 777 are less meaningful because they serve entirely different missions.
The Boeing 777 is a wide-body aircraft designed for long-haul international operations, carrying 300 to over 400 passengers along with substantial cargo payloads across intercontinental distances. Its acquisition costs, operating expenses and mission profile are vastly different from those of Embraer’s regional jets.
Rather than competing with wide-body aircraft, Embraer’s strength lies in providing economical service on short- and medium-haul routes where flexibility, frequency and lower trip costs matter more than maximum seating capacity.
If Adani eventually enters the airline business with an Embraer-centric fleet, it is unlikely to disrupt India’s narrow-body dominance on major trunk routes. Instead, it could reshape the country’s regional aviation landscape by connecting underserved cities, strengthening feeder networks into major hubs and creating an integrated aviation ecosystem linking aircraft manufacturing, airline operations and airport infrastructure.

articles.title: India’s eVTOL Startups Should Master Urban Air Mobility Before Chasing Regional Airliners
articles.text:
India’s emerging electric aviation ecosystem, led by companies such as The ePlane Company and BluJ Aerospace, has made significant progress in developing electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft for urban air mobility (UAM). As the sector matures, questions are increasingly being asked about whether these startups should skip the small-aircraft phase and instead develop 30–40 seater regional electric or hydrogen-powered aircraft.
While the long-term opportunity is compelling, making such a transition today would be strategically unsound and technically unrealistic. For most early-stage aerospace startups, attempting to leap directly from two- or four-seat eVTOL aircraft to regional commuter aircraft would expose them to enormous technological, financial and certification risks.
Aircraft carrying 30 to 40 passengers fall into an entirely different regulatory category than small eVTOL vehicles. They must satisfy stringent commercial airworthiness standards comparable to FAA Part 25 or EASA CS-25, requiring extensive structural testing, fatigue analysis, system redundancy validation, crashworthiness demonstrations and thousands of hours of flight testing. Completing such a programme typically requires investments running into hundreds of millions of dollars and development timelines extending well beyond a decade.
By contrast, today’s Indian eVTOL startups are focused on much smaller aircraft designed for intra-city mobility, emergency medical transport and logistics. Their engineering teams, manufacturing capabilities and funding structures are optimised for a very different class of aircraft.
For aircraft carrying 30–40 passengers over regional distances, current lithium-ion battery technology is not yet capable of delivering the required performance. Although battery energy densities continue to improve, they remain far below the energy available from conventional aviation fuel. The battery pack required to transport dozens of passengers over commercially meaningful distances would consume an impractically large share of the aircraft’s maximum take-off weight, leaving insufficient capacity for payload.
Whether used in fuel-cell electric propulsion or direct hydrogen combustion, hydrogen provides significantly higher specific energy than batteries, making it a more realistic zero-emission solution for regional aviation. However, adopting hydrogen introduces an entirely new set of engineering challenges.
Hydrogen must either be stored as a cryogenic liquid at extremely low temperatures or compressed at very high pressures. Both approaches require specialised tanks that occupy substantially more volume than conventional fuel systems, influencing aircraft configuration, centre-of-gravity management and aerodynamic design. Airports must also develop dedicated hydrogen production, storage and refuelling infrastructure before such aircraft can operate commercially.
Companies such as ZeroAvia have successfully demonstrated hydrogen-electric propulsion using modified regional aircraft, while other developers have explored similar concepts on aircraft such as the Dornier 228 and Dash 8. These programmes indicate that hydrogen-powered regional aviation is becoming increasingly feasible, but they also highlight the complexity of certifying entirely new propulsion architectures.
Many developers are pursuing a hybrid approach, combining hydrogen fuel cells for sustained cruise with batteries that provide the high power required during take-off and climb. Such architectures exploit the strengths of both energy sources while mitigating their individual limitations.
The current decade should remain focused on developing compact eVTOL aircraft serving urban air mobility, emergency medical services, cargo logistics and specialised commercial applications. These platforms allow companies to establish manufacturing capability, build operational experience and navigate aviation certification with comparatively manageable technical risk.
The next stage could involve expanding into larger unmanned cargo aircraft or hybrid-electric regional logistics platforms, enabling developers to gain experience with higher payloads, longer endurance and more sophisticated propulsion systems.
Only after achieving technological maturity, securing sustained funding and establishing industrial partnerships should Indian companies consider entering the regional commuter aircraft market. By the 2030s, advances in hydrogen propulsion, lightweight materials, fuel-cell technology and aviation infrastructure may create a commercially viable opportunity to develop indigenous 30–40 seater aircraft.
Such programmes would likely benefit from collaboration with established aerospace manufacturers, propulsion specialists and government agencies rather than being undertaken independently by early-stage startups.

articles.title: Could Kusha M1 Spawn a New Long-Range Air-to-Air Missile? The Numbers Behind the Debate
articles.text:
Following the successful first flight test of DRDO’s Kusha M1 interceptor and its notably sleek aerodynamic profile, defence enthusiasts and analysts have begun debating a tantalising possibility: could the M1’s airframe form the basis of a new, very long-range Indian air-to-air missile? The specific numbers being floated in this discussion — a roughly 250mm-diameter derivative reaching 250-350 km despite around 46% less propellant volume — are worth examining against what’s actually known about the M1’s design.
What the Kusha M1 Actually Is
The M1 interceptor is designed to neutralise threats at a range of 150 km, equipped with an Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) seeker, infrared and radio frequency guidance, and a dual-pulse solid rocket motor, giving it a single-shot kill probability exceeding 80 percent — and up to 98.5 percent in salvo mode. Built on the Akash-NG airframe, the M1 features a 250mm-diameter kill vehicle with thrust vector control, enabling high manoeuvrability at speeds up to Mach 5.5.
This 250mm figure is precisely the diameter being referenced in the current debate over a potential air-to-air derivative — since it’s already a known, compact, and aerodynamically refined missile body that has now been flight-validated as a functioning interceptor design.
The Case Being Made for an Air-to-Air Derivative
The core argument in this debate runs as follows: even if a hypothetical air-launched version of the M1 airframe loses roughly 46% of its propellant volume compared to the ground-launched surface-to-air variant — a plausible outcome if the booster stage is trimmed or removed since an aircraft-launched missile starts with far more initial velocity and altitude than a ground-based interceptor — the missile could still plausibly achieve somewhere in the 250-350 km range. The reasoning rests on three factors: retaining a dual-thrust (or dual-pulse) motor configuration for a sustained mid-course burn, lower aerodynamic drag from a cleaner airframe not burdened by ground-launch structural requirements, and the inherent kinetic energy advantage of being launched from a fast-moving, high-altitude aircraft rather than a stationary ground platform.
This is a coherent engineering argument in principle — air-launched missiles routinely achieve significantly greater range than their ground-launched booster-equipped counterparts using similar or even smaller rocket motors, precisely because the launch platform itself contributes substantial initial velocity and altitude that a ground-based system has to generate entirely through its own propulsion.
Why This Remains Speculative, Not Confirmed
It’s important to be clear about what this actually is: an informed technical discussion and debate among defence analysts and enthusiasts following the M1’s first flight test, not a confirmed DRDO programme. There is currently no official indication that DRDO, the IAF, or any associated laboratory is developing an air-to-air missile derived from the Kusha M1 airframe. The Kusha programme itself is explicitly structured as a ground-based air defence system — Project Kusha’s operational ranges are officially listed as M1 at 120-150 km, M2 at 250 km, and M3 at 350-400 km, all launched from Transporter Erector Launchers as part of a layered surface-to-air missile architecture.
What Would Actually Need to Change for an Air-Launched Variant
Converting a ground-launched interceptor airframe into a viable air-to-air missile is not a simple relabelling exercise. Beyond propellant and motor adjustments, such a conversion would typically require a redesigned seeker optimised for high-closure-rate air-to-air engagements rather than ground-launched intercepts of aerial threats, a different guidance and datalink architecture suited to fighter-radar cueing instead of ground-radar cueing, structural changes to handle the different stress profile of captive carriage and air launch, and integration work to fit the missile onto existing or planned Indian fighter pylons and weapons bays.
The M1’s existing dual-pulse solid rocket motor and blast fragmentation warhead — carrying approximately 2,500 fragments — are optimised specifically for defeating aerial targets at surface-to-air engagement geometries, which differ meaningfully from the geometry and closure rates typical of beyond-visual-range air-to-air combat. Adapting this seeker and warhead philosophy for genuine air-to-air use would likely require additional development work beyond simply repackaging the existing kill vehicle.
Why the Idea Isn’t Far-Fetched
That said, the broader premise isn’t implausible on its face. Cross-pollination between surface-to-air interceptor technology and air-to-air missile development is a well-established pattern globally — several long-range air-to-air missiles in service worldwide trace design lineage back to SAM programmes, since both weapon classes share core requirements around high-speed intercept, advanced seekers, and manoeuvrable airframes. The M1 and M2 interceptors already feature dual-mode seekers combining Electro-Optical/Infrared and active radar homing — a sophisticated guidance approach that would, in principle, translate reasonably well to an air-to-air role if adapted appropriately.
Given DRDO’s stated ambitions for extended-range air-to-air weapons for platforms like the Su-30MKI, Tejas Mk2, and AMCA, a Kusha M1-derived design is a technically reasonable direction for future study, even without any current official confirmation that such work is underway.

articles.title: Wildfire smoke now bigger prenatal threat than human sources of air pollution
articles.text:
In 1965, a presidential advisory panel issued a report warning that pervasive chemical and carbon pollution was harming environmental health and changing the climate. Five years later, President Richard Nixon signed the Clean Air Act.

Since that 1970 law and its amendments were passed, combined emissions of a half-dozen harmful air pollutants from vehicles and industrial sources have decreased by nearly 80 percent.

But mounting evidence shows that pollution from wildfire smoke is eclipsing those air-quality gains. The unchecked burning of fossil fuels is creating warmer, drier conditions that make wildfires more intense and destructive, and blanket communities in toxic smoke that is more harmful than pollution from other sources.

articles.title: Virgin Galactic flights stay paused while ticket prices head for the Moon
articles.text: Virgin Galactic has delayed its return to commercial spaceflight until February 2027, and plans to raise ticket prices later this year. The delay was disclosed alongside the company's financial results, which showed a net loss of $56 million for the second quarter of 2026, down from $67 million a year earlier. Revenue for the quarter was $0.1 million, compared to $0.4 million in 2025. According to CEO Michael Colglazier, demand exceeded the number of seats offered in the first $750,000 batch, prompting the company to prepare another at a higher price. Those customers will, however, have to wait a little longer. Colglazier said: "Our first ship is now expected to enter commercial service in February 2027 rather than the fourth quarter of 2026." He blamed the delay on the extra time needed to "complete avionics and systems installations." During an earnings call, Colglazier said: "No single issue is driving the schedule push. Rather, we have experienced modest time duration extensions across hundreds of relatively small but important installation tasks involved in the first build of our new spaceship." In response to an analyst question, Colglazier elaborated: "The number of those kind of 'Oh, we did not expect this to not fit just perfectly,' coming in is higher than we had allotted for. That just has started to accumulate on us. It really picked up at the tail end of July. For a bit, we thought we could manage that end, but the team just needed more time to do it the correct way." Integrated vehicle ground testing is expected to begin later in August, followed by flight testing in October. A second spaceship is due to join the fleet in March 2027, and the company expects to stop burning cash and "deliver positive quarterly cash flow within 2027." When Virgin Galactic reopened suborbital ticket sales in April, it charged $750,000 for a seat, up from the $600,000 price it cited in 2023. That was a substantial jump from the $100,000 envisaged more than two decades ago, when Sir Richard Branson announced plans for a scaled-up version of Burt Rutan's SpaceShipOne. At the time, the company said commercial flights would resume by the end of 2026. Virgin Galactic's last commercial flight took place in 2024, after which the company paused operations to focus on its next generation of spacecraft. Virgin Galactic is not alone in pausing its space-tourism service. Earlier this year, rival Blue Origin announced that New Shepard flights would pause for "no less than two years" while it worked on its crewed lunar program. ® Updated 8/18 at 10:19 GMT: A previous version of this story said that the program was "grounded," but the more appropriate term is "paused."
